title: More Vehicles Are Gaining Value and More Are Losing Value, but Most Are Still Flat

body_markdown:
The whole reason we watch the car market so closely, and why we update the[Hagerty Price Guide](https://www.hagerty.com/valuation-tools) four times a year, is because things are always, as Bob Dylan would say, “a-changin’.” Our latest update to the price guide went up in October, and we’ve already highlighted the big[winners](https://www.hagerty.com/media/market-trends/hagerty-insider/hagerty-price-guide/5-cars-gaining-value-in-a-split-market/) and[losers](https://www.hagerty.com/media/market-trends/5-vehicles-shedding-value-in-a-lopsided-market/) , surprising dips for popular[trucks](https://www.hagerty.com/media/market-trends/hagerty-insider/hagerty-price-guide/6-vintage-trucks-and-suvs-that-stumbled-last-quarter/) , and movement in the[muscle car](https://www.hagerty.com/media/market-trends/3-winners-and-3-losers-from-the-classic-muscle-car-market/) market over the previous three months. But it’s also useful to zoom out and look at the bigger picture, across the 39,811 cars and trucks that range from four-figure beaters to eight-figure blue chips.


Such scope gives a good indication of what’s going on across the many smaller markets that make up the collector car market as a whole. Below is a visualization of all the movement of all the cars and trucks in the Hagerty Price Guide, from January 2007 (the guide’s second edition) up to today. In red is the percentage of vehicles that decreased in value during each update. Gray is the percentage that stayed flat. Blue is the percentage that increased.


Typically, gray is the heftiest part of the graph, because as dynamic as the old car market is, most vehicles don’t change in value from one quarter to the next. They move more gradually. There are a few periods of exception, however, like the post-Great Recession shakeup and the 2022 peak of the pandemic boom, when the broader market has moved more quickly than normal.


The last time we took a close look at this graph, a[year ago](https://www.hagerty.com/media/market-trends/hagerty-insider/fewer-collector-vehicles-are-appreciating-and-most-are-flat/) , market observers and analysts were using words like “cooling” or “softening” to describe the market, and fewer vehicles in the price guide were going up in value than at almost any point in the guide’s history. Those words aren’t on anybody’s list in 2026, but the market is nuanced. Most vehicles (57%) still stayed flat over the quarter, but there has been a notable increase in the number of vehicles moving, and there’s a nearly even split between the ones going up (21%) and the ones going down (22%).


This points to the[mixed market](https://www.hagerty.com/media/market-trends/hagerty-indexes-underscore-a-mixed-market/) we’ve been covering for much of the year. “The shape of the collector car market has grown into two distinct segments,” says Greg Ingold, Senior Manager of Vehicle Valuations at Hagerty. “There are modern performance cars and supercars, the latter of which have exploded in value in 2026. Then there are the more traditional, long-established collector cars. Many of those are contracting in value following several years of growth after 2020.”


Collectors at the tip-top are driving big changes in six-, seven-, and eight-figure supercars as well as rare-spec, exceptional-condition examples of other modern vehicles. For the vast majority of enthusiasts, however, and the kind of people who buy cars for fun rather than profit, the market is far more rational, and there are buying opportunities to be had.
